stories.body: Saudi Arabia temporarily shut its 1,200km East-West pipeline after several drones launched from Iraq struck the route, causing injuries and damage that remain under assessment. The pipeline connects eastern oil facilities to Yanbu on the Red Sea and has become especially important as a way to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. Iraq acknowledged that the attack originated in Maysan province, dismissed the local operations commander and opened an investigation. Riyadh said it would not retaliate for now at Iraq's request, while reserving the right to protect its territory and energy infrastructure. The closure comes as Houthi gains around the Bab el-Mandeb add pressure to alternative oil-export routes, with crude prices rising above $100 a barrel.
stories.headline: Saudi Arabia shuts key East-West oil pipeline after drone attacks traced to Iraq

stories.body: Iran-aligned Houthi forces have captured Perim, or Mayun, Island in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait after government-allied forces withdrew, extending their rapid gains along Yemen's Red Sea coast. The island sits near the narrowest point of the waterway linking the Red Sea and Suez Canal to the Gulf of Aden, giving the Houthis greater ability to threaten or disrupt shipping. The group has also taken the port city of Mocha and substantial stretches of coastline, developments that deepen concern over global trade and energy flows as Iran retains influence over the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on the Red Sea route for oil exports amid disruption in Hormuz.
stories.headline: Houthis seize strategic Perim Island, tightening their grip on the Bab el-Mandeb shipping route

stories.body: Nearly 50,000 people have been displaced in Yemen's Taiz and Hodeidah governorates after a swift Houthi offensive captured towns along the Red Sea coast, according to the International Organization for Migration. Aid workers say families have fled shelling and shifting front lines with few belongings, while disrupted roads and communications complicate humanitarian access. The advance, which included the fall of Mocha, has raised fears of a return to wider civil war in a country already devastated by years of conflict and hunger. Urgent needs include shelter, food, clean water, healthcare, cash assistance and protection services.
stories.headline: Nearly 50,000 Yemeni civilians flee as Houthi forces advance along the Red Sea coast

stories.body: Leaders of the expanded BRICS grouping have opened a two-day summit in New Delhi, with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi hosting China's Xi Jinping, Russia's Vladimir Putin and Iran's Masoud Pezeshkian among others. The meeting is taking place amid the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, disruptions to energy and shipping, and pressure from US tariffs. Members are expected to discuss trade, investment, alternative cross-border payment systems and artificial-intelligence cooperation, but divisions within the larger bloc may limit a shared response to conflicts and economic policy. Xi's visit is his first to India in seven years, as the two countries seek to improve strained relations.
stories.headline: BRICS leaders gather in New Delhi as wars and US-China tensions test the bloc's unity

stories.body: Sweden votes on Sunday in a close general election that could return a centre-left bloc led by Social Democrat Magdalena Andersson or keep Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson's right-wing coalition in power. Kristersson has said the anti-immigration Sweden Democrats, which have neo-Nazi roots and currently support his government from outside the cabinet, could receive ministerial posts if the right retains power. Polls put the left narrowly ahead, though the margin has tightened. Migration, crime, national security, welfare spending and the economy dominate the campaign, while the prospect of the Sweden Democrats entering government has become a central question for voters.
stories.headline: Sweden heads to a knife-edge election with the far right seeking a role in government

stories.body: French investigators are examining suspected sabotage after a passenger train derailed near Cléon, south of Rouen, on Friday evening, injuring at least 44 people. An 18-year-old woman was airlifted to hospital in critical condition. Police reportedly found a fragment of rail on the track, though authorities have not announced a final cause. About 180 passengers were aboard the Rouen-Caen service, three carriages were reported to have overturned, and a mass-casualty response was activated. Rail operator SNCF said services in the area would face significant disruption.
stories.headline: French police investigate suspected sabotage in train derailment that injured at least 44 people

stories.body: The death toll from a fire aboard the MV June Aster in the Philippines has risen to 35 after the coast guard recovered 30 more bodies from the wreckage. The ferry caught fire on Wednesday near Coron after departing Manila, carrying passengers, crew and cargo on a 22-hour journey. Officials say the blaze appears to have started in the cargo hold and spread within seconds, leaving many passengers unable to put on lifejackets. Forty-three people have been rescued, while more than 50 remain unaccounted for; recovery crews expect the toll to rise as they continue searching the vessel.
stories.headline: Philippines ferry-fire death toll rises to 35, with dozens still missing

stories.body: Russia said it struck steel plants in Zaporizhzhia, Dnipro and Kryvyi Rih as well as two cargo vessels in the Black Sea port of Chornomorsk, continuing its campaign against Ukrainian industrial and logistics infrastructure. Ukrainian and Russian forces also exchanged long-range drone attacks, with Moscow reporting it downed 230 Ukrainian drones overnight and regional officials reporting damage and casualties. The strikes follow attacks on Kyiv fuel stations that Ukrainian officials say signal a new pressure campaign against civilian infrastructure. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has urged US President Donald Trump to impose new sanctions on Russia as US-led efforts to end the war remain stalled.
stories.headline: Russia strikes Ukrainian cargo vessels and steel plants as Zelensky urges Trump to impose new sanctions

stories.body: US annual inflation held steady in August, with the Labor Department's consumer price index rising as economists expected. The persistence of elevated prices leaves Republicans facing a difficult political backdrop heading toward the midterm elections, as voters continue to feel the effects of higher everyday costs despite an inflation reading that did not exceed expectations.
stories.headline: US inflation remains stubborn, leaving Republicans facing higher prices through the midterms

stories.body: Millions of federal student-loan borrowers could be moved into the most expensive repayment plan if they do not leave the SAVE program in time, but the transition process has been plagued by administrative snags. The Education Department's approach could sharply increase monthly bills for affected borrowers, while technical and processing problems make it harder for some to switch plans before the deadline.
stories.headline: Student-loan borrowers risk sharply higher payments as the SAVE transition encounters glitches

stories.body: Restaurants, hospitals and construction companies have begun layoffs as the future of temporary protected status for about 232,000 Salvadorans remains unresolved. Employers and workers face mounting uncertainty over whether affected residents will be allowed to keep working legally, raising concerns about labor shortages and disruption in industries that depend heavily on Salvadoran employees.
stories.headline: Businesses begin layoffs as the status of Salvadorans with temporary protected status remains uncertain

stories.body: Kamala Harris will campaign with Senator Jon Ossoff in Georgia and headline a Fulton County Democrats fundraising dinner in Atlanta next month, expanding her role in the midterm campaign. She is also scheduled to appear with Nevada attorney general and gubernatorial candidate Aaron Ford and with Democratic House challengers in California. Some candidates in more difficult states have kept their distance from the party's 2024 presidential nominee, but Harris says her immediate focus is helping Democrats regain control of Congress rather than deciding whether to seek the presidency again in 2028.
stories.headline: Kamala Harris plans to campaign with Senator Jon Ossoff in Georgia

stories.body: Gonzalo Sanz, the chief of staff to Spain's government delegate in Ceuta, has resigned amid a dispute over whether warnings from the intelligence service were passed on before a mass migrant crossing at the end of July. Declassified material showed that the CNI had alerted the local delegation to social-media calls to storm the border, but delegate Miguel Ángel Pérez Triano said he had not been informed. In his resignation letter, Sanz said he had told his superior and that reports documented warnings sent to ministries, adding pressure on the central government. Morocco has rejected accusations that it was responsible for the crossing and criticized Spanish politicians for using the crisis in domestic political disputes.
stories.headline: Ceuta migration crisis intensifies political pressure on Spain's government after a senior aide resigns

stories.body: Spain could lose between €800 million and €1.5 billion in pending EU recovery funds if parliament fails next week to ratify the government's emergency decree regulating lobbying, according to estimates cited by La Vanguardia. The reform is intended to meet a commitment tied to Spain's next €26 billion recovery-plan payment request, but the government does not yet have enough support. Junts plans to vote against the measure, while the People's Party has not set its position, and business groups and unions have criticized the proposal as overly bureaucratic. Brussels has repeatedly urged Spain to establish a mandatory public register for lobbyists.
stories.headline: Spain risks €1.5 billion in EU funds if its lobbying-regulation law fails

stories.body: Spain's Supreme Court has provisionally suspended voting rights for people who acquired Spanish nationality under the descendants law, prompting sharp criticism from the government and renewed allegations of electoral manipulation from the right. The court said there was a serious, substantiated risk that their inclusion could affect the transparency and objectivity of the electoral process, though the measure is temporary pending a ruling on the merits. Government ministers and PSOE figures said the decision unfairly discriminates against descendants of exiles, while Vox and PP leaders argued that the electoral roll had been improperly expanded.
stories.headline: Spain's Supreme Court ruling on the descendants law fuels an electoral-roll controversy

stories.body: Catalan independence groups brought 45,000 people onto Barcelona's streets for the Diada demonstration, according to the Guàrdia Urbana, while organizers put attendance at 100,000. The turnout was higher than last year's police estimate of 17,000. The march, organized by groups including the ANC and Òmnium Cultural, called for renewed unity and momentum for independence. ANC president Josep Vila announced plans for a major mobilization in autumn 2027, marking the tenth anniversary of the 2017 independence referendum, and said the organization would convene civil-society groups within a month.
stories.headline: Catalan independence movement draws tens of thousands on Diada and announces a major 2027 mobilisation

stories.body: Police arrested 18 people, including 10 minors, after violence following an anti-fascist Diada demonstration in central Barcelona. Mossos d'Esquadra said nine officers were lightly injured as groups set fire to containers and threw objects, stones, bottles, pyrotechnics and paint at police lines. The protest had been called to counter a gathering by the far-right Núcleo Nacional at Plaça Verdaguer; police kept the two groups apart before the anti-fascist crowd moved toward Arc de Triomf, where further clashes and dispersal operations took place.
stories.headline: Eighteen arrested after anti-fascist Diada demonstration in Barcelona turns violent

stories.body: Barcelona has received authorization to install 240 public-surveillance cameras in 2026, a sharp increase from the 150 authorized over the previous six years combined. The city has permission for 441 cameras in total, although it says only 186 are currently operating. Ciutat Vella accounts for 204 authorized devices, nearly half of the total, with La Rambla the single most monitored area. City officials say surveillance cameras will eventually reach every district, and the current government aims to have 500 cameras by 2027; installations require approval from Catalonia's video-surveillance oversight commission.
stories.headline: Barcelona expands video surveillance, with 240 cameras planned for 2026
